stem: A board member asks you to list the elements of a legally binding contract. Which set is correct?

options.text: Capacity, agreement (offer, acceptance, mutual assent), consideration, a lawful purpose and the correct form.
options.why: These are the five elements a KO must be able to recite: capacity, agreement, consideration, legality, and form.

options.text: Offer, acceptance, a signed SF 33 or SF 1449, and a certified funding document from the resource manager's office.
options.why: A specific form and a funding certification are contracting procedures, not the legal elements that make an agreement binding.

options.text: Competition, a fair and reasonable price, a responsibility determination, and a contract signed by both parties.
options.why: These are procurement policy requirements under the FAR, not the common-law elements of a contract.

options.text: Mutual assent and consideration only; capacity, legality and form are procedural preferences the courts may overlook.
options.why: Capacity, a legal purpose, and the correct form are elements in their own right, not optional preferences.

cite: Common law elements of contract formation; see also RFO FAR 2.101 (definition of contract)

stem: Under RFO FAR 1.405, what makes an agreement an unauthorized commitment?

options.text: It is not binding only because the person who made it lacked authority to bind the Government.
options.why: That is the regulatory definition; the only defect is the maker's lack of authority, which is why ratification can cure it.

options.text: It exceeds the contracting officer's warrant threshold, even though a warranted contracting officer signed it.
options.why: Exceeding a warrant is a different problem; the definition turns on the representative having no authority at all to bind the Government.

options.text: It was made without a certified funding document, so the obligation is void from the very start.
options.why: Missing funds raises Anti-Deficiency Act concerns, but the unauthorized commitment definition rests on lack of authority, not funding.

options.text: It is any contract later found to have an unreasonable price.
options.why: Price reasonableness is one of the ratification criteria, not the definition of an unauthorized commitment.

cite: RFO FAR 1.405 (was FAR 1.602-3)

stem: A facility manager directly called a Korean plumbing firm on a Saturday night to stop a burst water line and brings you an $18,000 invoice Monday asking you to "just pay it." What is the correct action?

options.text: Process it for ratification as an unauthorized commitment; at $18,000 the purchase card cannot be used.
options.why: The facility manager could not bind the Government, and at $18,000 the action is above the $15,000 micro-purchase threshold, so ratification is the path.

options.text: Pay the invoice on the purchase card because it was a genuine emergency and the facility manager is a cardholder.
options.why: The value exceeds the micro-purchase threshold, and neither an emergency nor holding a card gives the facility manager authority to bind the Government for this amount.

options.text: Refuse to act, since the Government never contracted and owes the vendor nothing.
options.why: The Government received the benefit of the repair; the proper course is a ratification review, and if it cannot be ratified the vendor's remedy is a claim under 31 U.S.C. 3702.

options.text: Issue a sole-source contract dated the prior Saturday to cover the work, citing the emergency.
options.why: Backdating a contract to cover a past act is improper documentation; the regulation provides ratification precisely so the record stays honest.

cite: RFO FAR 1.405; AFARS 5101.602-3-90; micro-purchase threshold $15,000 (RFO FAR 2.101); 31 U.S.C. 3702

stem: You suspect a contractor submitted a false claim on one of your service contracts. Under Army procedure, who do you contact first?

options.text: The Procurement Fraud Advisor, who sends a Procurement Flash Report up to the Procurement Fraud Branch.
options.why: AFARS 5109.406-3 and AR 27-40 chapter 8 put the Procurement Fraud Advisor at the front of the suspected-fraud channel.

options.text: The contractor's program manager, so the company can correct the invoice and refund any overpayment before anyone escalates.
options.why: Confronting the contractor risks destroying evidence and tipping off the subject; you do not investigate or confront.

options.text: The ethics counselor, because all fraud matters run through the Joint Ethics Regulation and the standards of conduct office.
options.why: The ethics counselor handles gratuities and personal conflicts of interest; suspected fraud goes to the Procurement Fraud Advisor.

options.text: The COR, who should gather statements and build a case file before legal or the investigators are involved.
options.why: The COR is not an investigator; you preserve the record and report the same day rather than running your own inquiry.

cite: AFARS 5109.406-3; AR 27-40 chapter 8; RFO FAR 3.104-7

stem: Which statement best captures why the contracting officer must fully document the contract file?

options.text: So someone else can pick it up and know its status, to comply with law and regulation, to defend your decisions, and to protect the Army in litigation.
options.why: Continuity, compliance, defensibility, and litigation protection are the four reasons a board expects to hear.

options.text: So the file can be destroyed sooner once the record retention clock starts.
options.why: Documentation supports retention and later review; it is not a way to shorten the retention period.

options.text: Because auditors require a complete file only on contracts above the simplified acquisition threshold, and smaller buys need just the order and invoice.
options.why: File documentation is required regardless of dollar value; there is no threshold that excuses it, even for small buys.

options.text: Because the contractor is entitled to a copy of the complete file on request under the Freedom of Information Act.
options.why: Contractors are not entitled to the full file, under FOIA or otherwise, and much of it is source selection or proprietary information.

cite: RFO FAR 4.101 (was FAR 4.801-4.803)

stem: An Army requirement includes commercial IT hardware and an access control system. Who is responsible for obtaining the ITAS approval?

options.text: The Requiring Activity, which submits the ITAS approval memo as part of the requirements package.
options.why: The RA obtains ITAS approval and includes it in the package, or submits an MFR signed by its ITAS Coordinator if approval is not required.

options.text: The contracting officer, as part of the acquisition plan, before the solicitation is released to industry.
options.why: The KO checks that the approval is in the package, but obtaining it is the requiring activity's responsibility.

options.text: The contractor, after award, as a condition of the first delivery order.
options.why: ITAS approval is a Government internal approval that precedes the requirements package, not a post-award contractor deliverable.

options.text: No one, because access control and CCTV systems are physical security equipment under the installation's provost marshal, not IT.
options.why: The AR 25-1 definition of IT is broad and expressly captures CCTV, fire alarm, access control, and intrusion detection systems.

cite: AR 25-1; Army ITAS approval policy

stem: Which contract types may a contracting officer use for a commercial product or commercial service acquisition under RFO FAR Part 12?

options.text: FFP or FP-EPA, with T&M allowed only under a determination and a ceiling; cost-reimbursement is prohibited.
options.why: RFO FAR 12.104 limits commercial contracts to FFP or FP-EPA, allows T&M only with a determination and ceiling, and bars cost-type.

options.text: Any contract type in Part 16 that the risk of the acquisition justifies, as with noncommercial buys.
options.why: That is the Part 15 rule; commercial acquisitions are deliberately restricted to fixed-price forms.

options.text: Cost-plus-fixed-fee whenever the commercial item requires minor modification for Government use.
options.why: Cost-reimbursement contracts are prohibited for commercial products and services regardless of modification.

options.text: Firm-fixed-price only, with no exceptions.
options.why: Fixed-price with economic price adjustment is also allowed, and T&M is available with a determination and ceiling.

cite: RFO FAR 12.104 (was FAR 12.207)

stem: You are deciding whether a proposed modification is within the scope of the existing contract. Which question is one of the recognized scope tests?

options.text: Would other firms have competed if the solicitation had described the modified contract?
options.why: The competitive-impact test asks whether the change would have drawn a materially different field of offerors.

options.text: Does the modification raise the price by less than ten percent of the original award value?
options.why: There is no fixed percentage test; cost change is one indicator considered with the nature of the work, not a bright line.

options.text: Has the contractor agreed in writing to the modification and waived any claim for more money?
options.why: Contractor agreement, with or without a waiver, makes a modification bilateral; it does not make an out-of-scope change lawful.

options.text: Is the contract still within its original period of performance and its original ceiling price?
options.why: Period of performance and price are factors to analyze, but staying inside them does not by itself keep a change in scope.

cite: RFO FAR 43 and 52.243-1 through 52.243-7; RFO FAR 6 (competition consequences of an out-of-scope change)

stem: Which of the following is an example of proposal information that may not be disclosed?

options.text: An offeror's indirect cost and direct labor rates.
options.why: Cost or pricing data, indirect costs, and direct labor rates are squarely within protected contractor bid or proposal information.

options.text: The name of the agency issuing the solicitation.
options.why: The issuing agency is public information published with the solicitation.

options.text: The evaluation factors stated in Section M of the solicitation.
options.why: Evaluation factors are disclosed to all offerors in the solicitation itself.

options.text: The total number of proposals received, after award has been announced.
options.why: The number of offerors received is routinely released in postaward notices and debriefings.

cite: RFO FAR 3.104 (procurement integrity); 41 U.S.C. chapter 21

stem: After award you receive a letter from an unsuccessful offeror objecting to the award in general terms, without using the word "protest." What do you do?

options.text: Send it to your legal advisor for an opinion on whether it is a protest and what to do next.
options.why: Whether an ambiguous letter is a protest is a legal determination with suspension and timeliness consequences, so legal reviews it.

options.text: File it in the contract file, since a protest must use the word "protest" to be valid.
options.why: No magic words are required; a letter can be a protest in substance, which is exactly why legal must review it.

options.text: Immediately suspend contract performance and notify GAO.
options.why: Suspension and GAO notification follow from a determination that a protest exists; you do not act before that determination.

options.text: Call the offeror and offer a second debriefing to resolve the concern informally.
options.why: An informal call does not address the legal status of the letter and can prejudice the record while a protest clock may be running.

cite: RFO FAR 33.104-3 (postaward agency protests); RFO FAR 33.105 (protests to GAO)

stem: What is the DoD's regulatory framework governing grants and cooperative agreements?

options.text: The DoD Grant and Agreement Regulations (DoDGARs).
options.why: DoDGARs is DoD's implementing regulation for assistance instruments, codified in title 32 CFR.

options.text: The Federal Acquisition Regulation, Part 35.
options.why: The FAR governs procurement contracts; assistance instruments are outside the FAR.

options.text: The Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement, Part 235.
options.why: DFARS supplements the FAR for procurement, not for grants and cooperative agreements.

options.text: The Army Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement, Part 5135.
options.why: AFARS is an acquisition supplement; the assistance framework is DoDGARs.

cite: DoDGARs, 32 CFR chapter I subchapter C; see also 2 CFR 200

stem: Which of the following is an example of an assistance instrument rather than a procurement instrument?

options.text: A Technology Investment Agreement.
options.why: TIAs, along with grants, cooperative agreements, and partnership intermediary agreements, are assistance instruments.

options.text: A Blanket Purchase Agreement.
options.why: A BPA is a simplified procurement method for repetitive supply and service needs, not an assistance instrument.

options.text: An indefinite-delivery, indefinite-quantity contract.
options.why: An IDIQ acquires supplies or services for the Government's direct benefit, which makes it a procurement contract.

options.text: A purchase order issued under simplified acquisition procedures.
options.why: A purchase order is a procurement instrument; its principal purpose is acquisition, not public support or stimulation.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 6303-6305; DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C)

stem: For a follow-on production contract or transaction to be awarded to prototype participants without competitive procedures, what must be true?

options.text: The prototype parties were chosen competitively, and the participants successfully completed the prototype.
options.why: Both conditions must be met: competitive selection up front and successful completion of the prototype.

options.text: The prototype was completed on schedule and within the original cost estimate, as certified by the program manager.
options.why: Schedule and cost performance, certified or not, are not the statutory conditions; competitive selection and successful completion are.

options.text: The senior procurement executive approves a justification for other than full and open competition before the award.
options.why: CICA and its justification machinery do not apply; the statute itself authorizes the follow-on without further competition.

options.text: At least one third of the production cost is paid from non-Federal sources.
options.why: The cost-share option is one of the eligibility conditions for using prototype authority, not a condition for the follow-on award.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4022(f) (formerly 10 U.S.C. 2371b(f))

stem: Which statement correctly describes how Federal statutes and regulations apply to Other Transactions?

options.text: Laws that apply only to procurement contracts, grants or cooperative agreements drop away, but other laws, such as fiscal and criminal law, still apply.
options.why: OTs are defined in the negative, so acquisition-specific law drops away while appropriations, security, export control, socio-economic, and criminal law still apply.

options.text: No Federal statutes apply, because an OT is a negotiated instrument outside the U.S. Code and is governed only by the terms the two parties agree and sign.
options.why: OTs are issued under statutory authority and remain subject to fiscal, criminal, security, and export control law, whatever the parties agree.

options.text: All FAR requirements apply unless the agreements officer writes a deviation and the senior procurement executive approves it.
options.why: The FAR does not apply to OTs at all, so no deviation is needed; any FAR-like term must be negotiated into the agreement.

options.text: Only the Contract Disputes Act and the Competition in Contracting Act apply.
options.why: Those are precisely the procurement statutes that do not apply to OTs.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4021 and 4022 (formerly 2371 and 2371b); DoD Other Transactions Guide

stem: Which of the following, standing alone, satisfies the eligibility condition for using prototype Other Transaction authority?

options.text: A nontraditional defense contractor or nonprofit research institution plays a significant part in the project.
options.why: Significant participation by a nontraditional or nonprofit research institution is the first of the four alternative conditions.

options.text: The prototype project is valued below the simplified acquisition threshold, so no approval above the agreements officer is needed.
options.why: Dollar value is not one of the eligibility conditions; it only affects the approval level.

options.text: The requiring activity certifies in writing that no FAR-based contract type could work for this prototype project.
options.why: A requiring activity certification is not a statutory condition; the four alternatives are set by statute.

options.text: The senior procurement executive waives the Competition in Contracting Act in writing for the prototype project.
options.why: CICA does not apply to OTs, so there is nothing to waive; exceptional circumstances require a written SPE determination instead.

stem: May costs a party incurred before an Other Transaction becomes effective be counted toward that party's contribution?

options.text: Yes, if incurred after negotiations began and an official finds in writing that they were incurred for the transaction and needed for its success.
options.why: The statute allows pre-effective-date costs to count only with that two-part written determination.

options.text: No, costs incurred before the effective date can never count toward a party's share.
options.why: The statute expressly permits them when the written determination is made.

options.text: Yes, automatically, because OT cost share is negotiated and not audited.
options.why: There is nothing automatic; the responsible official must determine and document both elements in writing.

options.text: Only if the costs were incurred before negotiations began, to show independent investment, and the agreements officer approves them in writing.
options.why: The statute reaches costs incurred after the beginning of negotiations, not before, whoever approves them.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4022 (formerly 10 U.S.C. 2371b), cost-share provisions

stem: Under ABG 75 procedures, how does "Brand Name or Equal" work?

options.text: The bidder must name and prove any "or equal" items; if it names none, it must deliver exactly what is specified.
options.why: The burden is on the bidder to name and prove equality, and silence binds the contractor to the specified brand.

options.text: The contracting officer must prove that the bidder's substitute is not equal before rejecting it, in writing to the bidder.
options.why: The proof of equality rests with the bidder, not the Government, however the rejection is written.

options.text: Any equivalent item may be substituted at any time during performance without notice.
options.why: Substitution must be identified and proven in the offer; it is not an open right during performance.

options.text: Brand name or equal is prohibited under ABG 75; only generic specifications may be used.
options.why: ABG 75 procedures recognize brand name or equal and set the rules for identifying and proving equal items.

cite: ABG 75 procedures (Germany); compare RFO FAR 11.204 / DFARS 211.204 (items peculiar to one manufacturer)

stem: When are funds actually obligated under a Blanket Purchase Agreement?

options.text: When each call is issued, not when the BPA is set up.
options.why: A BPA is not a contract and obligates nothing by itself; the obligation arises when the individual call or order is placed.

options.text: When the BPA is established, for the full estimated value.
options.why: Establishing a BPA creates no obligation; treating it as one would misstate available funds.

options.text: When the supplier delivers and submits an invoice.
options.why: Delivery and invoicing trigger payment, but the obligation is recorded when the call is issued.

options.text: At the end of the fiscal year, based on actual calls placed.
options.why: Obligations are recorded as calls are issued; year-end reconciliation does not create the obligation.

cite: RFO FAR 12.201-1 (BPAs under simplified procedures for commercial products and services; the RFO moved commercial simplified procedures out of Part 13 into Part 12) and RFO FAR 13 (simplified procedures for noncommercial acquisitions); 31 U.S.C. 1501

stem: What is the principal-purpose test that separates an assistance instrument from a procurement contract?

options.text: Assistance transfers value to support or stimulate a public purpose authorized by law; a contract buys property or services for the Government's direct benefit or use.
options.why: Principal purpose, support or stimulation versus direct Government benefit, is the statutory dividing line.

options.text: Assistance is used below the simplified acquisition threshold, and contracts are used above it, whatever the purpose of the award or the type of recipient.
options.why: Dollar value has nothing to do with choosing between assistance and acquisition; the purpose of the award decides.

options.text: Assistance is awarded to nonprofits; contracts are awarded to for-profit firms.
options.why: Recipient type does not control; a for-profit can receive assistance and a nonprofit can hold a contract.

options.text: Assistance is noncompetitive; contracts must be competed.
options.why: DoD policy maximizes competition in assistance awards too, so competition does not distinguish the instruments.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 6303 (contracts), 6304 (grants), 6305 (cooperative agreements)

stem: How must the availability of an assistance vehicle be announced?

options.text: Electronically: a synopsis at grants.gov linked to the full announcement on the Internet.
options.why: Notices must be electronic, and the grants.gov posting with a linked full announcement is the required channel.

options.text: By publication of a Notice of Funding Availability in the Federal Register, with no other posting.
options.why: A Notice of Funding Availability in the Federal Register is an additional optional format, not the required posting.

options.text: By direct solicitation of known principal investigators.
options.why: Direct approach to a recipient happens only where a statute directs it; it is not the general announcement method.

options.text: By posting in professional journals and their websites, which satisfies the electronic requirement.
options.why: Journal advertising, in print or online, is supplemental outreach and does not replace the required electronic posting.

cite: DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C); 2 CFR 200 announcement requirements; grants.gov

stem: Where is DoD assistance award information reported?

options.text: To the Defense Assistance Award Data System (DAADS).
options.why: DAADS is DoD's assistance reporting system and feeds statutory Federal reporting and management oversight.

options.text: To the Federal Procurement Data System, the same as contract actions.
options.why: FPDS-type reporting covers procurement actions; assistance awards report through DAADS.

options.text: To the Contractor Performance Assessment Reporting System.
options.why: CPARS records contractor past performance on contracts, not assistance award data.

options.text: Nowhere centrally; each Grants Officer retains the data in the award file.
options.why: Central reporting is required to meet statutory Federal reporting obligations.

cite: DoDGARs Part 21.535 (Defense Assistance Award Data System)

stem: Who may terminate an assistance award, and on what basis?

options.text: The Grants Officer for material noncompliance, both parties by agreement, or the recipient by written notice with reasons.
options.why: Those are the three recognized termination routes for an assistance award.

options.text: Only the Grants Officer, and only for the convenience of the Government.
options.why: Termination for convenience is a procurement concept; assistance terminations include mutual agreement and recipient-initiated notice.

options.text: Only the Head of the Contracting Activity, after a Grant Appeal Authority decision on the recipient's compliance.
options.why: The HCA sits as the appeal authority on claims; it is not the termination official.

options.text: Only the recipient, since assistance is voluntary participation.
options.why: The Grants Officer can terminate for material failure to comply, so the recipient is not the only party who can end the award.

cite: DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C); 2 CFR 200 termination provisions

stem: Should a Grants Officer seek competition in awarding grants and cooperative agreements?

options.text: Yes; DoD policy maximizes competition, and university research awards must use merit-based competitive procedures by statute unless exempt.
options.why: Competition is DoD policy generally and a statutory requirement for university research and research facility awards absent an exemption.

options.text: No; assistance awards are inherently noncompetitive because they support a public purpose, so the Grants Officer may pick the best-known recipient.
options.why: Supporting a public purpose does not excuse competition; DoD policy is to maximize it.

options.text: Only when the award exceeds the simplified acquisition threshold, as with procurement contracts, unless the program office waives competition.
options.why: No dollar threshold governs, and a program office cannot waive it; the policy and the statutory merit-based requirement apply regardless.

options.text: Only when more than one application is received.
options.why: Competition is sought up front through the announcement, not determined after applications arrive.

cite: DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C); statutory merit-based competition requirement for institutions of higher education

stem: A State agency holds a cooperative agreement. How does the Grants Officer obtain an audit?

options.text: The State gets a single audit from an independent auditor under government auditing standards, and the Federal Government relies on it.
options.why: The Single Audit Act places the audit duty on the recipient and directs Federal reliance on it.

options.text: The Grants Officer requests a DCAA audit of the State agency's incurred costs, the same way as for a contractor holding a cost-type contract.
options.why: DCAA audits contractors under procurement authority; the Single Audit Act route governs State recipients.

options.text: The Grants Officer performs the audit personally as part of post-award oversight, using the recipient's financial reports.
options.why: Grants Officers oversee and review; they do not conduct financial audits.

options.text: No audit is obtained, because States are exempt from Federal audit requirements.
options.why: States are not exempt; they are responsible for arranging the single audit.

cite: Single Audit Act; 2 CFR 200 subpart F

stem: In the OMB circular framework, which circular set the cost principles for State, local and Indian tribal government recipients before those principles were consolidated into 2 CFR 200 subpart E?

options.text: OMB Circular A-87.
options.why: A-87 set cost principles for State, local and Indian tribal governments; A-21 covered educational institutions and A-122 nonprofits. All three were consolidated into 2 CFR 200 subpart E, so answer the circular and then say where the principles live today.

options.text: OMB Circular A-21.
options.why: A-21 establishes cost principles for colleges and universities, not State and local governments.

options.text: OMB Circular A-122.
options.why: A-122 applies to nonprofit organizations.

options.text: OMB Circular A-76.
options.why: A-76 addresses commercial activities and public-private competition, not allowable costs on assistance awards.

cite: OMB Circular A-87 (State, local, tribal); A-21 (educational institutions); A-122 (nonprofits); see also 2 CFR 200 subpart E

stem: A recipient submits a claim that meets DoDGARs requirements. What must the Grants Officer do?

options.text: Decide in writing within 60 days, or give the date the decision will issue, citing the data relied on and the Grant Appeal Authority.
options.why: The 60-day written decision, the data relied on, and identification of the appeal authority are the required elements.

options.text: Issue a written decision within 60 days, citing the data relied on, and refer any appeal to the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals.
options.why: The Contract Disputes Act boards handle procurement claims; an assistance appeal goes to the designated Grant Appeal Authority.

options.text: Forward the claim to the servicing legal office, which issues the decision.
options.why: Legal advises, but the Grants Officer issues the written decision.

options.text: Take no action unless the recipient first certifies the claim over $100,000.
options.why: Claim certification thresholds are a Contract Disputes Act feature, not a DoDGARs assistance requirement.

cite: DoDGARs claim procedures; AFARS 5133.9001 (USACE Grant Appeal Authority is the HCA)

stem: Which of the following is one of the standards a recipient must meet to be qualified for a grant or cooperative agreement?

options.text: A satisfactory record of integrity and business ethics.
options.why: Integrity and business ethics sit alongside management capability, resources, past execution record, and legal eligibility.

options.text: Registration as a small business concern under the applicable NAICS code.
options.why: Small business size status is a procurement socioeconomic concept, not a recipient qualification standard.

options.text: An approved accounting system audited by DCAA.
options.why: The standard is adequate financial and technical resources and management capability, not a DCAA-approved system.

options.text: Prior receipt of at least one Federal award.
options.why: A prior award record is evaluated only if the applicant is a prior recipient; it is not a prerequisite.

cite: DoDGARs recipient qualification standards (see 32 CFR 22.420(c)); 2 CFR 200.206

stem: Must a DoD Component have statutory authority to make an assistance award?

options.text: Yes; assistance needs authorizing legislation, unlike a procurement contract, which agencies may use on inherent authority.
options.why: Assistance requires an authorizing statute; acquisition authority is inherent.

options.text: No; an appropriation alone is enough authority to make a grant, as long as the grant's purpose matches the appropriation act.
options.why: An appropriation provides funds, even for a matching purpose; the program still needs authorizing legislation to use an assistance instrument.

options.text: Only for grants; cooperative agreements may be awarded under general agency authority because the Government stays substantially involved.
options.why: Both instruments are assistance and both require authorizing legislation, whatever the Government's involvement.

options.text: No; DoDGARs itself supplies the authority for any DoD assistance award, because it is a regulation codified in title 32 of the CFR.
options.why: DoDGARs implements how assistance is awarded; a regulation in the CFR does not create the underlying program authority.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 6304-6305; DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C)

stem: Reviewing a local government's expenditures under a cooperative agreement, you find funds were used to buy staff tickets to a professional football game. What do you do?

options.text: Disallow it as unallowable entertainment, and consider an added audit or high-risk status with closer financial reporting.
options.why: Entertainment is unallowable under the applicable cost principles, and the finding justifies further audit or risk-based conditions.

options.text: Allow the cost if the recipient documents that the event was a team morale and retention activity approved by its director.
options.why: Entertainment costs such as sporting event tickets are unallowable regardless of the morale rationale or who approved them.

options.text: Terminate the award immediately for material failure to comply.
options.why: Termination is an enforcement option of last resort; the first step is disallowing the cost and adjusting oversight.

options.text: Refer the matter to the Grant Appeal Authority for a binding decision on allowability before taking any action on it yourself.
options.why: The Grants Officer makes the allowability determination; the appeal authority only hears an appeal from that decision.

cite: OMB Circular A-87 (State, local, tribal cost principles); 2 CFR 200 subpart E

stem: What are the three types of Other Transactions?

options.text: Research, Prototype, and follow-on Production.
options.why: Research OTs, prototype project OTs, and noncompetitive follow-on production OTs are the three recognized types.

options.text: Research, Cooperative Research and Development Agreements, and Prototype.
options.why: A CRADA is a separate instrument; an OT is by definition not a CRADA.

options.text: Prototype, Production, and Technology Investment Agreement.
options.why: A TIA is an assistance instrument under DoDGARs, not one of the three OT types.

options.text: Basic research, applied research, and commercial solutions openings.
options.why: A commercial solutions opening is a solicitation vehicle, not a type of Other Transaction.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4021 (research, formerly 2371); 10 U.S.C. 4022 (prototype, formerly 2371b); 10 U.S.C. 4022(f) (follow-on production)

stem: Can a Grants Officer execute an Other Transaction the way they execute a grant or cooperative agreement?

options.text: No; an OT is not a contract, grant, cooperative agreement or CRADA, and a warranted Agreements Officer signs it.
options.why: OTs are defined in the negative and require an Agreements Officer with the appropriate warrant.

options.text: Yes; grants officer authority covers all non-FAR instruments.
options.why: Grants Officer authority reaches assistance instruments, not Other Transactions.

options.text: Yes, but only for research OTs, since those most resemble assistance and are awarded to universities.
options.why: Even research OTs are Other Transactions and require Agreements Officer authority, whoever the recipient is.

options.text: No; only a warranted contracting officer may sign an OT, using the same warrant that covers FAR contracts.
options.why: A KO warrant is not the instrument of OT authority; the Agreements Officer warrant is.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 4021 and 4022 (formerly 2371 and 2371b); DoD Other Transactions Guide; Army Warranting Program Policy v12 (MAR 2026)

stem: What makes an entity a nontraditional defense contractor?

options.text: For at least the year before the solicitation, it has held no DoD contract or subcontract under full CAS coverage.
options.why: The statutory test is the absence of a full-CAS-covered DoD contract or subcontract in the preceding year.

options.text: It has never held a prime contract or a subcontract of any kind with the Department of Defense or any of its components.
options.why: Prior DoD work, prime or sub, is permitted; what matters is no full-CAS-covered work in the preceding one-year period.

options.text: It qualifies as a small business under the applicable size standard.
options.why: Small business status is a separate category; a large firm can be nontraditional and a small firm may not be.

options.text: It is a commercial firm that sells only to the commercial marketplace and has never accepted Government contract terms.
options.why: The definition does not require exclusively commercial sales or a clean record of Government terms, only the absence of full-CAS-covered DoD work in the past year.

cite: 10 U.S.C. 3014 / 4022 nontraditional defense contractor definition (Section 815, FY2016 NDAA); 41 U.S.C. 1502 (Cost Accounting Standards)

stem: Which of these does NOT apply to an Other Transaction Agreement?

options.text: The Truth in Negotiations Act and the Contract Disputes Act.
options.why: Procurement-specific statutes such as TINA, the CDA, CICA, Bayh-Dole and the procurement protest system do not apply to OTs.

options.text: Federal fiscal law, including the purpose and bona fide need rules.
options.why: Fiscal law applies fully to OTs; appropriations discipline is never waived.

options.text: Criminal law on false claims and false statements.
options.why: Criminal statutes apply to OTs like any other Government dealing.

options.text: Export control and limited distribution restrictions.
options.why: Export control and distribution restrictions apply because they are not acquisition-process statutes.

cite: DoD Other Transactions Guide; 10 U.S.C. 4021 and 4022 (formerly 2371 and 2371b)

stem: Is market research required before awarding an Other Transaction?

options.text: Yes; the D&F supporting the OT summarizes the market research, including outreach to nontraditional defense contractors.
options.why: The D&F must capture the market research and the outreach strategy aimed at nontraditional participation.

options.text: No; FAR Part 10 does not apply to OTs, so no market research is performed and the D&F covers only the prototype's purpose.
options.why: FAR Part 10 does not apply, but market research is still required and documented in the D&F.

options.text: Only for prototype OTs above the senior procurement executive approval threshold.
options.why: The requirement is not tied to a dollar tier.

options.text: Only if a consortium is not being used, because the consortium manager does the outreach.
options.why: Consortium use does not excuse market research, whoever does the outreach; the D&F still captures it.

cite: DoD Other Transactions Guide; Determination and Findings in support of an OTA

stem: How are intellectual property rights handled on an OT prototype project?

options.text: Bayh-Dole does not apply; IP rights are negotiated for each project by the agreements officer, requiring activity and IP counsel.
options.why: IP terms are negotiable on each OT, which is why IP counsel involvement is essential to support follow-on development.

options.text: The DFARS data rights clauses apply by operation of the Christian doctrine, as they would in any FAR-based research or prototype contract.
options.why: The Christian doctrine reads clauses into FAR contracts; it does not reach Other Transactions, whatever the project.

options.text: The Government always receives unlimited rights in all technical data delivered, since it funds most of the prototype project work.
options.why: Nothing is automatic in an OT, even when the Government funds most of the work; unlimited rights would have to be negotiated and paid for.

options.text: The contractor always retains all rights, and the Government receives none.
options.why: Rights are whatever the parties negotiate, which can and often should include rights supporting follow-on production.

cite: DoD Other Transactions Guide (intellectual property); 10 U.S.C. 4022 (formerly 2371b)

stem: In the order of precedence governing grants and cooperative agreements, which source controls over the others?

options.text: Federal statutes and law.
options.why: Law trumps all, followed by Federal regulations, executive orders and circulars, then agency regulation, then standard and award-specific terms.

options.text: Award-specific terms and conditions negotiated with the recipient.
options.why: Award-specific terms sit near the bottom of the order and cannot override statute or regulation.

options.text: Agency regulation such as DoDGARs.
options.why: Agency regulation ranks below Federal statutes and Federal regulations, executive orders and circulars.

options.text: Standard terms and conditions published in the award package.
options.why: Standard terms rank below law, Federal regulation, and agency regulation.

cite: DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C); 2 CFR 200

stem: Under 31 U.S.C. 6304 and 6305, what distinguishes a cooperative agreement from a grant?

options.text: Both transfer value for a public purpose of support or stimulation, but only a cooperative agreement expects substantial agency involvement.
options.why: The principal purpose is identical; substantial involvement is the sole statutory difference.

options.text: A grant transfers money while a cooperative agreement transfers property or services, such as equipment on loan.
options.why: Both transfer a thing of value; the form of the value is not the distinction.

options.text: A grant is for state and local governments, while a cooperative agreement is for universities and nonprofit research groups.
options.why: Recipient type does not determine the instrument; substantial involvement does.

options.text: A cooperative agreement acquires property or services for the Government's direct use.
options.why: That is the definition of a procurement contract under 31 U.S.C. 6303.

cite: 31 U.S.C. 6304 (grants); 31 U.S.C. 6305 (cooperative agreements)

stem: How does the authority of the Grants Officer's Representative compare to that of the Grants Officer?

options.text: The GOR advises on technical matters; only the Grants Officer issues or changes the award and approves exceptions.
options.why: The GOR advises on technical matters and performance; decision authority over the award stays with the Grants Officer.

options.text: The GOR may approve extensions to report due dates as long as no funds change and the Grants Officer is copied on it.
options.why: Approving exceptions such as extended report submission is expressly a Grants Officer authority, copied or not.

options.text: The GOR may modify the statement of work when technical direction is needed, if the change stays within the budget.
options.why: Any change to the award, including scope, requires a Grants Officer modification, even within budget.

options.text: The GOR and the Grants Officer share equal authority over the award, each one within their own part of the agreement.
options.why: The Grants Officer holds ultimate authority for decisions related to the award.

cite: DoDGARs (32 CFR chapter I subchapter C); 2 CFR 200 post-award administration

stem: You are helping a Grants Specialist apply the pre-award risk review under 2 CFR 200.206. Which source do you check for prior terminations and negative integrity information about the applicant?

options.text: FAPIIS, together with suspension and debarment status.
options.why: FAPIIS carries termination history and other integrity information, and exclusion status restricts awards and subawards.

options.text: CPARS narrative ratings on the applicant's prior contracts.
options.why: CPARS covers contractor performance on procurement contracts, not the assistance risk review sources named in 2 CFR 200.206.

options.text: The Defense Assistance Award Data System.
options.why: DAADS is the reporting system for award data, not a source of integrity or termination findings.

options.text: The recipient's own certification in its application, which is conclusive.
options.why: Self-certification does not replace the agency's independent review of available information.

cite: 2 CFR 200.206 (Federal awarding agency review of risk posed by applicants); FAPIIS

stem: What is the Logistics Cost Sharing (LCS) Program?

options.text: Part of the Special Measures Agreement, the U.S.-ROK cost-sharing deal, that partly offsets USFK logistics costs.
options.why: LCS sits inside the SMA and offsets logistics costs such as movement of personnel and assets, repair and maintenance, and non-tactical vehicle purchases.

options.text: A U.S. appropriation that reimburses the ROK for base construction and relocation costs on the peninsula.
options.why: LCS is ROK-provided support under the SMA, not a U.S. appropriation flowing to the ROK.

options.text: A NATO-style host nation support agreement administered by the Defense Logistics Agency for all U.S. forces in Asia.
options.why: LCS is a Korea-specific SMA program managed by USFK J4, not a DLA program for the region.

options.text: A working capital fund the 411th CSB uses to finance local purchases in Korea.
options.why: LCS funds are held by ROK MND, not in a U.S. working capital fund.

cite: U.S.-ROK Special Measures Agreement; USFK LCS Program (confirm current program guidance with C&P)

stem: Who ultimately approves and awards an LCS contract, and what is the 411th CSB contracting officer's role?

options.text: ROK MND approves and awards the contract; the 411th KO makes a recommendation for award through USFK J4.
options.why: LCS funds stay with ROK MND, USFK J4 manages the program, and the KO recommends rather than awards.

options.text: The 411th CSB contracting officer awards the contract and ROK MND reimburses the United States.
options.why: Funds are never transferred to the U.S., and the KO does not award LCS contracts.

options.text: USFK J4 awards the contract and the 411th KO administers it.
options.why: J4 manages the program, but the approval and award authority rests with ROK MND.

options.text: The Head of the Contracting Activity awards it after ROK MND concurrence.
options.why: The HCA has no award role in LCS; ROK MND approves and awards.

cite: USFK LCS Program under the Special Measures Agreement; 411th CSB LCS workflow (confirm current procedures with C&P)

stem: Which of the following is a limitation on the use of LCS funds?

options.text: The program is limited to local Korean businesses, and Korean material and labor must be used.
options.why: LCS competition is limited to Korean firms and the program requires Korean material and labor, with offshore or local material documented to J4.

options.text: LCS contracts may only be awarded below the simplified acquisition threshold, with larger needs paid from O&M.
options.why: There is no such ceiling; LCS actions can be large and require the corresponding approvals and source selection planning.

options.text: LCS contracts must be competed among U.S. and Korean firms on an equal basis, as with any SOFA procurement.
options.why: LCS competition is limited to Korean contractors, which is why it cannot be mixed with full and open O&M competition.

options.text: LCS funds expire at the end of the U.S. fiscal year like O&M.
options.why: LCS funds are ROK funds held by ROK MND, not U.S. annual appropriations.

cite: USFK LCS Program guidance; J4 offshore/local material memo requirement (confirm current guidance with C&P)

stem: Can a single solicitation be funded with both O&M and LCS funds?

options.text: No; O&M needs full and open competition while LCS is limited to Korean firms, and one solicitation cannot carry both rules.
options.why: The two funding streams impose incompatible competition rules, so they cannot share a solicitation.

options.text: Yes, if the contracting officer documents a justification for other than full and open competition for the O&M part.
options.why: A justification does not reconcile two contradictory competition requirements in one solicitation.

options.text: Yes, as long as separate contract line items are used for each fund type.
options.why: Separate CLINs do not fix the competition conflict, which attaches to the solicitation as a whole.

options.text: Yes, with ROK MND approval, since MND awards the LCS portion.
options.why: MND approval does not change the competition rules that govern the U.S. solicitation.

cite: RFO FAR 6 (competition requirements); USFK LCS Program guidance (confirm current procedures with C&P)

stem: In the SOFA Invited Contractor program, who is responsible for each step of obtaining IC status?

options.text: The contracting officer gets the contract's SOFA designation from USFK/FKAQ; the requiring activity gets each individual's designation.
options.why: It is a two-step process with the KO handling the contract-level designation and the RA handling the individual designation.

options.text: The contractor applies directly to the ROK government for both designations.
options.why: The request for contract SOFA designation goes from the contracting officer to USFK/FKAQ.

options.text: The requiring activity obtains both the contract designation and the individual designations from USFK/FKAQ, since it owns the requirement.
options.why: Contract-level designation is the contracting officer's responsibility, even though the requiring activity owns the requirement.

options.text: The contracting officer obtains both designations from USFK/FKAQ as part of contract administration, after the contractor arrives in Korea.
options.why: Individual contractor designation is the requiring activity's step, whenever the contractor arrives.

cite: SOFA Article XV; USFKI 4901.01; USFK/FKAQ Invited Contractor program (confirm current procedures with C&P)

stem: A customer brings you a procurement package for a new ABG3 action. Which set of documents would you tell them is vital to include?

options.text: PR&C, DA Form 4283, Service Contract Approval, a description of the action, the IGE, the repair to replacement ratio, and a secondary services justification.
options.why: These are the package elements the customer must supply for a new ABG3 action.

options.text: Only a PR&C and a statement of work; the contracting office then develops the estimate, the approvals and every justification it needs from those two documents alone.
options.why: The requiring activity owns the estimate, approvals, and justifications, not just the funding and work description.

options.text: A PR&C, a DD Form 254, and a small business coordination record.
options.why: A DD Form 254 covers classified performance and small business coordination is a different process; neither is the ABG3 package core.

options.text: A DA Form 4283 and a sole source justification signed by the requiring activity, since ABG actions are noncompetitive by design.
options.why: ABG actions are not inherently noncompetitive, and the package needs the IGE, approvals, and ratio and services justifications as well.

cite: ABG 75 procedures (Germany); 409th CSB local ABG package requirements (confirm current requirements locally)
